title: Ship Real Agents: Hands-On Evals for Agentic Applications — Laurie Voss, Arize
talk_summary: Laurie Voss explains how to instrument agent traces, read real failures, and build code evals, LLM-as-judge rubrics, golden datasets, and experiments to improve agents. The core loop is trace -> eval -> human annotate -> analyze -> improve, with meta-evaluation to validate judges and regression suites to safely change prompts/models.

takeaways.what_they_do: Instrument every agent/tool/LLM call as spans, then read real traces before writing evals to categorize failures and root causes.
takeaways.evidence_quote: traces record what your AI did. Every agent call, every tool call, every LLM invocation

takeaways.what_they_do: Write cheap deterministic checks for schema, required fields, forbidden phrases, and expected entities before using LLM judges.
takeaways.evidence_quote: They run in milliseconds and because they are just code, they cost basically nothing to run.

takeaways.what_they_do: Use separate LLM judges per dimension with explicit criteria, labeled examples, binary labels, and chain-of-thought instead of one god evaluator.
takeaways.evidence_quote: Instead, uh split your evaluator into one thing per dimension.

takeaways.what_they_do: Build human-labeled golden dataset, compare judge predictions to it, compute precision/recall, and tune rubric; prioritize recall for review gates.
takeaways.evidence_quote: An eval that you haven't validated is just a fancy way of being wrong at scale.
takeaways.numbers: toy judge: precision 100%, recall low; 2/6 human-judge disagreements

takeaways.what_they_do: Run a fixed eval suite on same inputs/evaluator when changing model or prompt; only ship if regressions pass.
takeaways.evidence_quote: you can just run a regression and know whether or not it is safe to upgrade

takeaways.what_they_do: Measure accuracy divided by cost and use tiered models: cheap for simple queries, expensive for complex ones.
takeaways.evidence_quote: It is accuracy divided by cost.
